stages.notes: CV screen is harsh without elite pedigree (top-20 filter is real). Recruiter phone follows online OA: location/fit (East Coast trading hubs), current role, and why trading.

Online math assessment first: expectation/distributions; ~10–20 MCQs covering probability & stats (dice, balls, cards), calculus, and linear algebra. Then quant phone: concept depth — explain yourself; when stuck, narrate how you get unstuck. Tech round still uses basic programming problems.

Senior-quant data exercise: pretend trading dataset + prompt. Deliverable is a concise report — not a 200-graph notebook. Careful prioritization; explain method and results; anticipate 'why doesn't your analysis see X?'

Open-ended probability & statistics and game-theory style thinking questions — decompose on the fly. Fly-out presentation of the data exercise: show something new and defend it to a math-PhD audience. Intern loop mirrors FT; internship is often an 8-week version of the same interview bar.

processNotes: Finance background not required up front — math, probability, and clear thinking matter more.
Brevity is highly valued on the data exercise: results first, method second, no chart spam.
Day-to-day signal to use in fit rounds: quoting into the market, retuning parameters, modelling/valuation, shipping systems with developers, urgency of live trading.
Phone and onsite score how you think out loud; partial progress with structured stuck-handling beats silent perfection.
Public prep narratives cite Ross (Introduction to Probability Models), Bailey (problem-solving probability), and introductory derivatives pricing texts.

questions.text: Online assessment: expectation and distribution questions (geometric waiting times, conditional probability) plus calculus and linear algebra MCQs — dice, urns/balls, and cards are common toys.
Walk through a classic conditional-probability puzzle (e.g. Monty Hall or a variant with changing information). Explain your reasoning step by step.
Solve a probability or expectation problem involving dice, cards, or urns. The interviewer may give hints — practice narrating your thought process while you work.
Linear algebra or calculus question at the level of eigenvalues, matrix intuition, or optimization — explain concepts, not just compute.
You're stuck mid-problem. Narrate how you get unstuck: smaller case, invariants, what you'd try next. Interviewers score the process, not silence.
Short programming exercise or live coding: implement a small algorithm or data structure and talk through complexity and edge cases.
Recruiter screen: where do you live / work, and are you open to on-site collaboration at the firm's East Coast trading hubs?
Walk through your research or industry background and why you want a trading / options market-making desk.
Take-home: load a trading or market-style dataset with Python/pandas, clean anomalies, and produce a concise report with a few decisive findings — not dozens of exploratory plots.
In the data-exercise write-up: explain how you got each result and what it means. Anticipate a senior asking why your analysis does not see a particular effect.
Open-ended probability / statistics question — decompose under time pressure; show structured reasoning and sanity checks.
Game-theory / competitive-strategy style puzzle: invent a winning theory on the fly (payoffs, information, strategies) and bound or compute.
Present your data-exercise findings: prefer one novel, PhD-defendable insight over a tour of every chart.
Culture fit: how you collaborate on hard problems, handle ambiguity, and communicate technical work to non-specialists.
Tech interview: basic programming problem — correct solution, edge cases, and complexity. AI-era tooling does not remove this round.
